rationale: A wins because it knows which absences are stories and which are land mines. Its sharpest line, "Warby Parker says store shoppers spend more than online buyers. It will not say how much," turns the thin company claim into a real reporting assignment. B keeps dressing broad DTC nostalgia as news with "Warby Parker was supposed to make optical stores obsolete," then adds a shaky workforce angle that asserts more than the update gives it.
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker built its brand on skipping the middleman" leans on brand history not supplied in the update; usable, but it needs confirmation before pitching.
"The company that made direct-to-consumer eyewear a category" is an outside-history claim, not a provided fact.
"puts pressure on whoever currently sells eyewear in pharmacies and on incumbent optical chains" is plausible strategy color, but still an inferred competitive effect, not evidence from the update.
gaps_in_B: "Warby Parker was supposed to make optical stores obsolete" is a big founding-premise claim not in the update. This is where the contrarian angle starts freelancing.
"the post-DTC reckoning" and "DTC survival argument" are trend wrappers looking for proof. The update gives Warby facts, not a category verdict.

"Warby Parker's retail expansion means a large new employer of optometrists" overstates the fact pattern. The update says most new stores will have optometrist-staffed exams; it does not say employment model, hiring volume, or workforce impact.
"pharmacy-as-healthcare-hub trend" and "where Americans can get optical care" stretch a glasses-selling pilot into healthcare access before the partner, locations, or exam pathway are known.
